P6616:
# Icosapent ethyl for hypertriglyceridaemia and atherosclerosis: greater RESPECT for increased therapeutic use

**Authors:** Prakriti Gaba; Deepak L Bhatt; William E Boden

**Affiliations:** 1 Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 2 Mount Sinai Heart, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, 1 Gustave Levy Place, Box 1030, New York, NY 10029, USA | 3 Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Icosapent ethyl (IPE) for hypertriglyceridaemia—what are the pros and cons? In this graphical abstract, we highlight the pros and cons of IPE for the management of hypertriglyceridaemia, discuss the key results of three major clinical trials exploring the role of IPE or eicosapentaenoic acid on cardiovascular outcomes in subjects with hypertriglyceridaemia, and summarize practical considerations for clinicians considering IPE use in practice.

Hypertriglyceridaemia is an important risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. With a prevalence of >10% in the adult population, hypertriglyceridaemia remains a significant burden in the cardiovascular community.1 A variety of pharmacotherapeutic agents have been developed to target elevated triglyceride levels and to potentially mitigate the adverse cardiovascular sequelae that often accompany them. These agents include focused triglyceride-lowering agents, such as high-dose omega-3 fatty acids, fibrates, and niacin, as well as LDL-cholesterol-lowering medications, including statins and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin 9 inhibitors. Omega-3 fatty acids with highly purified pharmaceutical grade eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), or icosapent ethyl (IPE), have been of particular interest, given their ability to reduce adverse cardiovascular events.

To date, three clinical trials have explored the role of IPE and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with various degrees of hypertriglyceridaemia on background statin therapy—JELIS, REDUCE-IT, and most recently, RESPECT-EPA.2–4 Yet, despite the wealth of information provided by these multi-centre trials, the rates of utilization remain low.

One factor that may have limited uptake of IPE was the postulation that the use of pharmaceutical grade mineral oil may have interfered with the absorption of statins. There have also been some concerns regarding the higher rates of hospitalization for atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter (3.1% vs. 2.1%, P = .004) and bleeding (2.7% vs. 2.1%, P = .06), respectively, with IPE compared with placebo.3 In addition, other factors contributing to limited uptake of IPE may be related to its affordability and the overall pill burden for patients.5 Herein, we highlight the increasing evidence that challenges these criticisms and supports the use of IPE in the treatment of patients with hypertriglyceridaemia and elevated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk.

First and foremost, three randomized clinical trials have illustrated the clinical benefit of EPA and IPE, as have at least four prospective imaging studies.6,7 In JELIS, for instance, which was the first of the three clinical trials of EPA or IPE to be reported, 18 645 patients recruited from Japan between 1996 and 1999 were randomized to receive either 1.8 g/day of IPE plus a statin vs. a statin alone.2 Eligible patients were required to have total cholesterol concentrations of 6.5 mmol/L (∼251 mg/dL) or greater and were excluded if they had an acute myocardial infarction (MI) in the past 6 months. Among enrolled patients, the median triglyceride level was ∼1.73 mmol/L (or ∼153 mg/dL). Thus, nearly half of patients had triglyceride levels under 150 mg/dL. There was a 19% relative reduction in major coronary events in all patients treated with EPA plus a statin versus those treated with a statin alone (P = .011).2 In the primary prevention subgroup, EPA treatment was associated with an 18% reduction in major coronary events (P = .13) and in the secondary prevention subgroup, EPA treatment was associated with a 19% reduction in major coronary events (P = .048). Among all patients, there were also lower rates of individual endpoints, with a 24% statistically significant reduction in unstable angina, and numerically, although not significantly, lower rates of fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and coronary death.

In 2019, the landmark REDUCE-IT trial extended the findings of JELIS by showing, for the first time in a randomized placebo-controlled trial, that treatment with a higher dose of 4 g/day of IPE (2 g twice daily) was associated with a 25% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events.3 A detailed hierarchical analysis showed that reductions in individual endpoints were also substantial and statistically significant, with a 31% reduction in fatal or non-fatal myocardial infarction, 20% reduction in cardiovascular death, and a 28% reduction in fatal or non-fatal stroke. Moreover, the salutary benefits were present regardless of baseline triglyceride levels. Although RESPECT-EPA, the most recent of the three clinical trials, was underpowered and failed to meet statistical significance in its primary endpoint, it too revealed a 21% lower rate of the primary outcome (a composite of cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, unstable angina requiring hospitalization, and revascularization) among patients treated with IPE, despite a lower treatment dose (1.8 g of IPE daily) than what was used in the REDUCE-IT trial.4 There was also a statistically significant 27% reduction in the incidence of the secondary composite endpoint of sudden cardiac death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, and coronary revascularization (P = .031). Nonetheless, the findings from RESPECT-EPA should be interpreted with caution as there are several limitations to consider. These include, but are not limited to, its open label, as opposed to blinded design, the high rates of drug discontinuation during the study period, and the limited generalizability of the trial findings, given the narrow study population. Patients studied in RESPECT-EPA consisted primarily of those with a low EPA/arachidonic acid ratio (<0.4), i.e. those with higher levels of inflammation. Whether these findings would also apply to patients with lower levels of inflammation seen in general practice is less clear from the existing trial results.4

Beyond the accumulated evidence of clinical event reduction associated with IPE, there is an important biochemical basis that supports its benefit. Recent experimental work has shed light on its mechanism of action.8 Specifically, EPA has been shown to incorporate itself into the phospholipid bilayer of cells, decreasing lipid oxidation and reducing inflammation. This characteristic of EPA contrasts with docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), another agent commonly found in omega-3 combination formulations, which does not have this ability nor a clinical cardiovascular benefit. DHA, unlike EPA, increases lipid bilayer instability and fluidity. In endothelial cells, EPA has additionally been associated with reduced platelet aggregation and leukocyte adhesion.9,10 By competing with omega-6 fatty acids for cyclooxygenase enzymes, EPA produces thromboxane A3 and decreases the production of thromboxane A2—a potent atherothrombotic agent.8 EPA also increases the release of nitric oxide, promoting vasodilation and decreasing vasospasm, in addition to a reduction in plaque volume and the enhanced generation of specialized inflammation-resolving mediators.10 The combination of these positive attributes has, in meta-analyses, been associated with reduced cardiovascular mortality and improved cardiovascular outcomes with EPA vs. EPA + DHA.11

While there has been debate about the magnitude of risk reduction benefit in REDUCE-IT which was attributable to the use of mineral oil placebo,12,13 the safety and utility of pharmaceutical grade mineral oil as a placebo has been extensively explored in prior clinical trials along with a host (∼80) of other prospective and retrospective studies, and its use as a control has been deemed acceptable by regulatory agencies.14,15 Moreover, recent work comparing EPA with mineral oil or corn oil in vitro demonstrated that, while EPA produced a significant reduction in the rate of LDL oxidation, there was no change with mineral or corn oil, supporting the inert nature of this placebo.9

Although there are reports of increased atrial fibrillation and bleeding with IPE, these risks do not outweigh the clinical benefits afforded by IPE administration in the right clinical scenario, as the majority of cases of atrial fibrillation occurred in patients who had a prior history of the condition. Moreover, bleeding in all trials was mostly minor, such as skin bruising, with no significant excess in fatal, intracranial, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary bleeding.3 Thus, the preponderance of evidence supports the net clinical benefit of IPE in reducing incident cardiovascular events with very low rates of off-target adverse effects.

Finally, recent cost-effectiveness analyses in the USA have demonstrated that for high-risk patients with hypertriglyceridaemia despite statin treatment, IPE may be a cost-effective therapy at commonly accepted willingness-to-pay thresholds at a cost of $4.16–$9.28 per day, although analyses are needed in other regions.16

In summary, we now have evidence from an amalgamation of sources, such as randomized clinical trials, prospective imaging studies, and basic science experiments, that support the use of IPE in the treatment of patients with even mild hypertriglyceridaemia and elevated cardiovascular risk.17 The US Food & Drug Administration has approved IPE as an adjunct to maximally tolerated statin therapy for mitigating cardiovascular risk in patients with triglyceride levels ≥150 mg and either established cardiovascular disease or diabetes plus additional cardiovascular risk factors. The risks of the medication are few and the benefits substantial. As such, the main therapeutic focus moving forward should be enhanced implementation of this therapy in appropriate patients.
